item.title: The recipe is the dataset
item.dc:creator: Michael Sumner
item.description:
A 3 MB text file makes 5800 cloud-optimized GeoTIFFs behave like one dataset at every scale, from a whole continent at 1 km down to a single valley at 2 m. GDAL has been able to read such a file for years. What is new is that a web page can read it too, the same way, with no server in between, and keep an honest account of what every view costs.

I built (with llm) a REMA explorer to expose what I’d been doing to read REMA at any scale, mostly in R. Building it shows: most of what we want from a viewer is already possible, and the hard question is not what can be done but how the pieces should be grouped and packaged.

Every tile streams, the continent does not

The Polar Geospatial Center publishes REMA v2 as tiles: 5800 COGs at 2 m, each about 50 km across, and 1523 each at 10 m and 32 m, 100 km across. Every one of them is a well-made COG. It has internal overviews, so reading a 50 km tile at low resolution is cheap.

But the overviews stop at the tile edge. A view of a 500 km glacier basin touches hundreds of files; a view of the continent touches all 5800, and each one costs at least a header read. The whole-continent mosaics at 100 m, 500 m and 1 km exist, but only inside tarballs. There is no single thing you can point a reader at and ask for “Antarctica at 1 km”.

The fix is a recipe, not a payload. REMA-2m_dem_ovr.vrt mosaics all 5800 2 m COGs by URL and declares five <Overview> entries: PGC’s own 10 m and 32 m VRTs, then three coarse COGs copied out of the tarballs (100 m as Int16 with sparse tiles, 500 m, 1 km). When a read asks for fewer pixels than the 2 m grid, GDAL picks the overview that fits, exactly as it would inside a single file. The fine data never moves; the only new payload is the cheap end of the pyramid.

gdalwarp -tr 1000 1000 /vsicurl/https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mdsumner/rema-ovr/main/REMA-2m_dem_ovr.vrt rema_1km.tif

That command and its 2 m twin over one small box both read a bounded number of bytes, because the warper chooses the level for you.

The browser can be the warper

The explorer fetches that same VRT and does what the warper does, per screen tile, in five steps:

  1. Pick a level. The display grid is EPSG:3031 with 256 px tiles at 8192 / 2^z m, the same origin as NASA’s polar GIBS tiles. For a tile at resolution R, take the coarsest level whose pixel is no larger than 1.5 R.
  2. Find the files. For a VRT level, a bucket index over the DstRect footprints gives the files that touch the tile.
  3. Pick an image inside each file. Same rule again: full resolution or one of its internal overviews.
  4. Read only the window. Compute the pixel window and ask geotiff.js for those blocks. Single-range requests need no CORS preflight.
  5. Sample into the tile. Nearest, or bilinear when upsampling, using each file’s own georeferencing.

Nothing is precomputed. There is no tile cache, no server and no index other than the VRT. The page is a reader of the recipe, the same recipe GDAL, R and Python read.

It also keeps a ledger: requests, bytes and seconds for every settled view. A whole-continent view reads a few megabytes from the coarse overviews of the 1 km file. A 60 km coastal view reads one or two megabytes of the 100 m file. A view at 2 m reads a few blocks of one or two tiles. The area on screen spans six orders of magnitude; the cost does not. That is the whole argument, measured rather than claimed.

What the usual stack bakes in

None of this is exotic, so it is worth asking why it feels new. The answer is that most tools fuse decisions that should stay separate. Each fusion is reasonable on its own, and each one closes a door.

Baked-in decision What it costs What the recipe approach does instead
Pre-rendered tile pyramids are the storage A second copy of the data, styled once, frozen at the build date The source COGs are the storage; tiles are a view computed on demand
Web Mercator is the map Polar data is distorted or clipped, and the poles are second-class Each dataset is read in its own CRS; the display grid is a choice, here EPSG:3031
A server makes the tiles Infrastructure to run, and the client only ever sees pictures The client is the warper; the server is a static file host
Overviews live inside the file You cannot add a pyramid to data you do not own External overviews in a VRT add a pyramid to anyone’s data by reference
Style is baked into pixels Changing a ramp means re-rendering; a hover shows a colour, not a value Tiles hold values; colour, hillshade, slope, contours and equalisation are functions applied at draw time
One viewer per question The 2D map, the profile tool and the 3D view are separate programs with separate readers One read function serves all of them

Even GDAL has a baked-in assumption worth knowing: it treats an overview as covering exactly the extent of the base raster. The 1 km and 500 m files here start 900 m and 400 m outside the 2 m grid, and the 32 m VRT is offset by up to 20 m. GDAL therefore misregisters those levels by up to about one of their own pixels at the edges. The browser reader uses each file’s own geotransform and does not. It is a small thing, and exactly the kind of thing that only shows up when you build the machinery yourself.

Same technology, different gears

Every community in this space uses the same parts: COGs, HTTP range requests, GDAL and PROJ. What differs is the gear they work in, and each gear makes different things easy.

The R spatial community works close to GDAL. A DSN string, the warper and a VRT are everyday tools, and packages like vapour, gdalraster, terra and stars expose the warper and the target grid directly. “This extent at this size” is one call, and target_dim = c(1024, 0) lets GDAL work out the other side. That habit is why a recipe like this VRT feels ordinary there rather than clever.

The cloud-native trend in Python works a gear up, on chunked arrays: xarray over Zarr, byte references harvested into kerchunk or VirtualiZarr, Icechunk for versioned stores, and tile services such as TiTiler for the web. odc-geo’s GeoBox is the same grid idea under another name. In JavaScript, geotiff.js, OpenLayers and deck.gl move reading and rendering into the client. These gears are strong for analysis at scale and for services with many users.

The gears differ most at the seams. REMA’s 2 m tiles overlap their neighbours by 100 px (200 m), and the 10 m tiles by 20 px. To a VRT, and to this page, that is harmless: the shared pixels are painted twice with the same value, a no-op. To a Zarr store the same overlap is real work. A regular chunk grid cannot describe tiles that start 25000 px apart but are 25100 px wide, and the 512 px blocks inside them do not line up from one tile to the next. Virtualizing it means trimming the overlaps and adopting a rectilinear (variable-size) chunk grid, which Zarr is still standardizing.

Multiscale is the same story. Geospatial Zarr is still converging on how to describe a pyramid, through GeoZarr and the multiscales conventions that follow the microscopy world’s OME-NGFF precedent, and each level has to be written as its own array. A VRT has had this for years: an <Overview> entry points at any other dataset, a file or another VRT, and a mosaic can even mix sources at different resolutions, because each source carries its own scaling from source to destination pixels. That is not a criticism of the Zarr work, which is solving real problems for analysis at scale. It is a reminder that some of what is being engineered as a new paradigm already exists, quietly, one gear down, and that the two can meet: a byte-reference index over these same COGs is just another recipe.

Neither gear is wrong. The lesson is to keep the grid and the recipe at the bottom, where every gear can reach them, and to choose the gear per question rather than per community.

One primitive, many policies

The explorer has one primitive: give it a grid (an extent, a resolution, a size) and it returns an array of values. Everything else is a policy about which grid to ask for, or what to do with the answer.

  • The map asks for 256 px tiles that match the screen.
  • Point info asks for a 1 x 1 grid at every level’s native pixel, so one click shows the same spot through the whole pyramid.
  • A profile asks for tiles at the resolution of its sample spacing.
  • A box asks for up to 1024 px across, then hands the result back as a GeoTIFF and as a GDAL, Python or R recipe for the same grid.
  • The globe asks for one texture-sized grid and drapes it on the WGS84 ellipsoid. REMA heights are ellipsoidal, so exaggeration 1 is geometrically exact.

The level choice is a policy too. Auto mimics the warper; pinning a level reads it at its native pixel size at every zoom, so you see its real pixels. Comparison is the same machinery run twice and swiped. The tile-boundary overlay draws the same index the reader uses: the source files, the 512 px blocks of the overview actually read, or the display tiles, either following the level of detail or fixed to one level.

That last one matters more than it looks. Most viewers hide their machinery. Showing it, as an ordinary layer you can switch on, turns a viewer into an instrument: you can see which file answered, which overview was chosen and what it cost. Because each feature is a policy over the same primitive, adding one never touches the others. The globe did not need a second reader; the cutaway did not need a third.

What an honest reader exposes

A reader that refuses to fake things finds the gaps in the data, not just in the tools.

  • Products with no pyramid. PGC also publishes per-pixel count, MAD and min/max date beside every tile. They exist only at 2 m, 10 m and 32 m, so a continent view would mean touching every file. The explorer draws them when you zoom in and says no when you zoom out. That refusal is the argument for building their overviews too.
  • Storage type shows through. The Int16 100 m overview terraces in 1 m steps, and on flat ice a hillshade at high exaggeration makes that visible. The coarse Float32 overviews with LZW compression are larger than they need to be, and the ledger shows it.
  • Vertical datums collide. The globe cutaway along the 44 km line from Little Dome C (Beyond EPICA) to Dome C North (the AAD Million Year Ice Core site) drops a wall from the REMA surface to the Bedmap2 bed: about 3 km of ice. But Bedmap2 heights are relative to a geoid and REMA’s to the ellipsoid, so the thickness carries an offset of tens of metres. The picture makes you notice; a pipeline would not.
  • Hosting is part of the design. The fine levels only work in a browser if their bucket sends CORS headers. GitHub LFS serves the coarse levels with them, and GitHub release assets do not. Every byte read through LFS counts against a bandwidth quota. These are not footnotes; they decide what a page can see.

Refactoring toward new ways of seeing

If the capabilities are already there, the work is in where the seams go. Four layers fell out of building this, and each can change without the others.

  1. Storage is bytes in COGs, wherever they live: PGC’s bucket, an LFS file, a release, a bucket of our own. It should know nothing about who reads it.
  2. Index is the recipe: a VRT today, a byte-reference Parquet or a STAC catalogue tomorrow. It is small text, versioned like code, and it is where a pyramid is added to data you do not own.
  3. Planning answers “for this grid, which level, which files, which blocks?” It is a pure function of the index and the grid. It is also the part worth making visible, because it is where cost is decided.
  4. Rendering turns arrays into pictures: colour, shading, a profile chart, a mesh. It never reaches past the planner to the bytes.

Two habits make the layers hold. First, make the grid the unit of every request. An extent and a dimension is something GDAL, R, Python and a browser all understand, and target_dim = c(1024, 0) lets the tool work out the rest. Second, package by question, not by app. A map, a profile, a box and a globe are not four programs; they are four grids asked of one reader, and a new question should be a new policy, not a new stack.

What comes next follows from the layers. Move storage to a bucket and keep the index in git. Build the missing pyramids for the sibling products. Swap Bedmap2 for Bedmap3 on the same vertical datum, then the cutaway shows true thickness. And let the display CRS be a choice rather than a given, which is where reprojection belongs: in rendering, never in storage.

Grouping, not capability

Every feature in the explorer was possible before it existed: pyramid-aware reads, polar display, hillshade, profiles, boxes, imagery swipes, a globe, a cutaway. What had been missing was a way of grouping them so that each stays small and none gets in another’s way. One reader, grids as requests, policies on top, the machinery on show and a ledger beside it.

The recipe is the dataset. Keep it small, keep it readable by every tool, and the ways of seeing it can keep multiplying without anyone copying the data again.

  • Explorer: mdsumner.github.io/rema-ovr, source in mdsumner/rema-ovr
  • Howat, I., Porter, C., Smith, B. E., Noh, M.-J., and Morin, P.: The Reference Elevation Model of Antarctica, The Cryosphere, 13(2), 665–674, 2019. Data from the Polar Geospatial Center

Earlier pieces this draws on, each one a single idea from the list above:

  • Warp and cell: two worlds that were never separate (this site, 2026-10-06): names the recipe-not-payload principle this post builds a working reader around
  • rangefinder: Sentinel-2 composites from STAC, read and stretched in the browser, no tile server
  • ortho-cog-viewer: COGs reprojected on the fly with a mesh, the display CRS as a choice
  • lunamap: basemaps, coordinates in several forms, and elevation profiles from a 2 m DEM
  • aatgrid: a parametric tile scheme, the grid as an explicit, shared object

item.title: Where the line falls: tensors, tables and four layers
item.dc:creator: Michael Sumner
item.description:
Arguments about geospatial and scientific data often come down to tensors versus tables: Zarr against Parquet, datacubes against feature collections, raster against vector. This essay argues that there is no single line between them. Storage, indexing, topology and rendering each draw the line in a different place, so the same dataset is a tensor from one layer and a table from another. Seeing the four lines separately makes several recurring design problems easier to name, and suggests that the two sides need each other more than they compete.

One model underneath

Almost every dataset in this field can be described the same way: a set of values over an index space, plus a map from each index to a place. A sea surface temperature grid has an index of (row, column, time) and a map that turns a row and column into a longitude and latitude. A table of ship positions has an index of row numbers and a map that is simply two of its columns.

The map comes in two kinds.

  • Implicit. The map is a recipe: an origin and a cell size, an affine geotransform, a start and a step, a rule that turns a HEALPix cell id into a cell on the sphere. Nothing per cell is stored; any cell’s place can be computed.
  • Explicit. The map is stored: arrays of longitude and latitude, a column of geometries, a table of vertices and the triangles that connect them.

Tensors and tables are the two ends of this scale. A tensor is a table whose key is implicit. Its index is complete and cartesian, so every combination of row, column and time exists and its coordinates follow from the recipe. A table is a one-dimensional tensor whose key is explicit. Its rows are indexed by number, the meaningful coordinates are ordinary columns, and nothing is implied about rows that are absent.

The interesting data sits between the ends. A curvilinear ocean model grid has a complete index but no recipe for its coordinates, so they are stored. A table of satellite granules can have a column whose every value is itself an array: a “dimensional column”. A ragged collection of float profiles is a table of profiles, each holding a short tensor.

None of this is new. Visualization software settled the same taxonomy in the 1990s. VTK’s dataset types run from fully implicit to fully explicit: ImageData (an origin and spacing), RectilinearGrid (one coordinate vector per axis), StructuredGrid (explicit coordinates on a complete index), UnstructuredGrid (explicit points and cells) and PolyData (points, lines and polygons). Geographic software split along the same scale into raster and vector, and for a long time treated the two halves as separate worlds with separate tools.

Four layers, four lines

A data system has at least four layers, and each has its own version of the tensor and table split. Communities tend to see the whole ecosystem divided along the line their own layer draws.

Layer Tensor side Table side What the line really is
Storage Zarr, Icechunk, netCDF and HDF5, COG Parquet, Iceberg, Arrow, GeoPackage Chunked by index space, or by rows
Index Implicit maps: affine transforms, ranges, HEALPix ids Explicit maps: coordinate columns, geometry columns, spatial trees over stored shapes Whether a place is computed or looked up
Topology Structured: neighbours implied by the index Unstructured: neighbours recorded as vertices, edges and faces Whether connectivity is implied or stored
Rendering Warp: an image is moved to the view as a whole Cell: each cell or feature becomes geometry and is drawn When the map is applied: late, on the GPU, or early, as geometry

Storage is where the argument is usually held, and it is the least fundamental of the four. Zarr chunks values by blocks of index space; Parquet chunks them by groups of rows. Either can carry the other three layers. UGRID mesh connectivity is routinely stored as integer arrays in netCDF or Zarr, and the index of a collection of raster files is routinely stored as a table.

Index is the layer that decides how a coordinate becomes a position, and back. It is where the implicit and explicit maps live. Xarray’s recent work on pluggable indexes makes this layer explicit in code: since version 2025.6 an index is a replaceable component, and a CoordinateTransformIndex computes coordinates from a function rather than storing them.

Topology is about neighbours. In a regular grid the neighbours of a cell follow from its index; in a triangular mesh they have to be recorded. A HEALPix grid is structured in this sense even though it is not rectangular.

Rendering is where the two kinds of map meet the screen. A warp-based viewer keeps an image whole and moves it into the view’s projection, applying the map as late as possible. A cell-based viewer derives a geometry for each cell or feature and draws those, applying the map early. Both draw the same data, and in practice both are converging on the same datasets.

Objects that change sides

Because each layer draws its own line, the same object is a tensor from one layer and a table from another. This is why debates about the split rarely settle: the participants are standing in different layers.

Object As a tensor As a table
Triangular mesh (UGRID) Connectivity arrays and values over a face dimension, in netCDF or Zarr Tables of vertices, edges and triangles
Ocean float profiles Contiguous ragged arrays (CF conventions) One row per observation, or per profile with an array column
HEALPix field A one-dimensional array over cell ids, with an implicit map A sorted table of cell id and value, possibly sparse
Mosaic of COG files Tiles of one large implicit grid A tile index with one row per file and its footprint
Chunk byte references The chunk grid of a Zarr array Rows of path, offset and length (kerchunk’s Parquet references)
Vector data cube An n-D array with one dimension indexed by geometries A feature table with a time dimension per feature
Curvilinear model grid Values on a complete (i, j) index One stored longitude and latitude per cell, with no recipe

Two of these deserve a closer look.

A mesh is arrays to the model that writes it and tables to the software that edits it. Neither view is wrong. They are the same relations with the joins either implied by array position or written out as keys.

Byte references are a table whose only purpose is to describe a tensor. Each row says where one chunk of an array lives in some file. It is the clearest case of the two sides needing each other, and it comes back in the cases below.

Case: catalogs are tables in disguise

STAC, the SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog, is written as a tree of JSON documents. Normalized, it is three or four tables, joined by keys that the JSON leaves implicit in its nesting:

Table Key What a row holds
Collections collection id Extent, license, summaries
Items item id, collection id Datetime, footprint geometry, properties
Assets asset key, item id Link, media type, roles; with the projection extension, proj:shape and proj:transform
Bands band index, asset Scale, offset, nodata, statistics (raster:bands, eo:bands)

The tree form makes this structure hard to see in four ways.

  • Joins become position. An asset belongs to whatever item encloses it. There is no column to join on until the tree is flattened.
  • One viewpoint is built in. The tree is item-centric. “Every red-band asset sharing this transform” is a natural query on a long assets table and an awkward walk through documents.
  • The schema is per document. Extensions may add fields anywhere, so there is no table-wide schema to normalize against.
  • Identity becomes addresses. Links are URLs rather than keys.

stac-geoparquet goes a long way: one row per item, in a columnar format that query engines read directly. Assets are typically kept as a nested column keyed by asset name, so the tree survives one level down and the schema varies from collection to collection.

Once normalized, an asset row with proj:shape and proj:transform is an array descriptor: a shape plus an implicit map from index to place. Add a table of byte references keyed by asset and chunk, and the catalog and a virtual array store turn out to share one relational schema, viewed from opposite ends.

Catalog relation Array-store relation
Collection Repository, or a top-level group
Item A group per scene
Asset, band An array
Byte references A chunk manifest

This matters for a live design question: how to store Level 2 data, the per-scene products that do not share a grid. A talk at CNG Forum 2026 by Tom Nicholas (Earthmover) and Sean Harkins (Development Seed) proposes keeping many scenes, of any shape and projection, as separate groups in one Icechunk repository, alongside a STAC-like metadata table, so that catalog and data change in one atomic commit. The motivation is real and well argued: when a catalog and its files live in separate systems, a failed job can leave files no search will find, and a reprocessing run can leave catalog entries pointing at deleted files. The talk shows two prototypes for the table, one storing columns as one-dimensional Zarr arrays read through DataFusion, and one placing an Apache Iceberg table’s pointer in the repository’s commit metadata. It also reports that virtualizing the full Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 archive this way implies about 7.7 billion repository nodes, with commit cost currently growing with node count, and that the fix is in progress.

Seen through the layers, this design records the scene-to-array relation twice: once as the repository’s hierarchy, and once in the catalog table. The normalized view above suggests an alternative worth exploring alongside it, in which the catalog, the array descriptors and the byte references are all ordinary tables, and arrays are what their rows point to. Which side should hold the transaction is an open question, and both approaches are likely to teach something.

Case: self-indexing formats and references

A recent DuckDB post describes a database file with no data in it: only view definitions that query Parquet files elsewhere, on object storage or over HTTPS. The file stays a few hundred kilobytes however large the data grows, and acts as a shareable catalog. Each view’s reference is the text of a query, such as read_parquet('s3://...') over a file pattern. There are no byte ranges in it.

That works because Parquet indexes itself. A Parquet file’s footer records where every row group and column chunk sits, with minimum and maximum statistics. A reader that knows only the file can still fetch just the bytes a query needs. References at the granularity of whole files are enough.

Many array formats are not like this. In HDF5, and so in netCDF-4, locating a chunk means walking internal B-trees, which costs many small reads before any data arrives. That is why byte-reference harvesting exists: kerchunk, VirtualiZarr, Icechunk’s virtual chunks, and tools that ask GDAL’s multidimensional API for chunk locations all build, ahead of time, the table of path, offset and length that the format does not offer cheaply. Read that way, a harvested reference table is the footer those formats are missing.

The idea is older than any of these. A GDAL VRT is a small file of references and transforms over data that lives elsewhere, and has been since the early 2000s. The line runs from VRT through kerchunk to DuckDB views: a catalog that describes data instead of holding it.

All of these share one requirement that is easy to forget: the referenced data must not change. A view over a file pattern silently returns different results when files are added or rewritten. A byte reference into a file that has been replaced points at the wrong bytes. References are safe when what they point to is pinned: a versioned object, a snapshot, a content-addressed chunk, or a fixed list of immutable files.

Case: what to do with a swath

A satellite swath is the hardest case for the tensor side. Each granule has its own footprint, often in the sensor’s own geometry, with a stored longitude and latitude for every pixel. Granules overlap, and no two share a grid. There are three honest ways to hold a collection of them.

  1. One group per granule, plus a catalog. Every granule keeps its own arrays and its own explicit coordinates, and a table indexes them. Nothing is lost or resampled. The granules never become one array, and any cross-granule view has to be assembled when it is requested.
  2. Resample to a common grid. Every granule is binned or interpolated onto one grid, producing a cube. This is how Level 3 products are made. It answers many questions well, but it is a different product: the original observations, and their individual footprints, are gone.
  3. A global implicit index. Assign every observation the id of the discrete global grid cell it falls in (HEALPix, S2, H3 or similar), and store rows of (cell, time, value), with whatever per-observation detail is needed. The map from index to place is implicit and shared by every granule. Observations are not resampled. Overlaps simply become several rows for one cell. The result is a table and a sparse tensor over a global cell dimension at the same time.

The third option sits squarely between the two sides, which is why neither side tends to propose it. It also fits the idea of dimensional columns: one row per granule or scan line, carrying its footprint, time and geolocation recipe as ordinary columns, with arrays as the payload of each row.

Who works on which layer

Most projects cover one layer well, some two. A partial and certainly incomplete map:

Layer Python Rust and TypeScript R and others
Storage zarr-python, Icechunk, VirtualiZarr, kerchunk Icechunk core, icechunk-js, async-tiff, obstore GDAL multidimensional API, gdalraster, ncdf4, Rarr; hypertidy’s blocklist and altarr
Index xarray pluggable indexes: rasterix, xproj, xvec, xdggs geoarrow-rs stars; hypertidy’s vaster and grout
Topology UXarray, xugrid, meshio spade, CDT (C++) MDAL, CGAL; sf and wk for features; hypertidy’s meshcore, silicate and trianglewins
Rendering GeoVista (on PyVista and VTK), lonboard deck.gl-raster, gridlook mapview, tmap

The xarray index work is the closest anyone has come to writing the index layer down as code. Meshes are the next frontier there: UXarray and xugrid treat a mesh as a grid object beside xarray rather than as an index within it, and whether a mesh can be an index is open. On the rendering side, GeoVista carries VTK’s dataset taxonomy into earth science directly, and is perhaps the clearest statement of the model in this essay from the visualization end.

Open questions

These are questions, not conclusions. Each could be answered by building something small.

  1. Should references be open tables? If byte references were ordinary Parquet or Iceberg tables, every query engine could read them, and a reference table could double as the catalog. What would be lost relative to references held inside an array store?
  2. Where should the transaction live? Consistency between catalog and data needs one commit protocol. An array store can host a table, or a table format can point into arrays. Which composes better with the engines people already use?
  3. Can a mesh be an index? If a mesh could be an index in the way an affine transform now is in xarray, meshes and rasters would share selection, alignment and concatenation.
  4. What is the smallest shared index contract across languages? Python now has one in xarray. R has no pluggable equivalent: the map from index to place is tied to the classes of individual packages. A small contract for computed coordinates would let packages interoperate without sharing classes.
  5. How should pinning be expressed? Every reference system depends on immutable sources, but there is no common way to state that a reference is pinned, or to check it.
  6. Is the swath problem a table problem? If collections of granules are tables first, with arrays as the payload of rows, how much of the Level 2 difficulty goes away, and what new difficulty appears?

Sources

  • Xarray blog: flexible indexing (September 2025)
  • Announcing rasterix.RasterIndex
  • Gallery of xarray custom indexes
  • UXarray: supported models and grid formats
  • xugrid
  • GeoVista
  • xvec: introduction to vector data cubes
  • Level 2 Data Collections in Zarr, CNG Forum 2026 (slides) and slide source
  • zarr-datafusion-search
  • Icechest
  • Icechunk issue 2449: commit memory and total nodes
  • DuckDB: a database with no data in it (October 2026)

item.title: Warp and cell: two worlds that were never separate
item.dc:creator: Michael Sumner
item.description:
Two globes

Open two browser tabs, both live at sidebyside. In one, gridlook draws a month of EERIE model precipitation on a globe: 196,608 HEALPix cells, each placed on the sphere and coloured, spinning under the mouse. In the other, ortho-cog-viewer draws a Sentinel-2 scene of eastern Tasmania on an oblique Mercator centred wherever the screen centre happens to be, rewarping as you pan. Both are static HTML on a free host, both read their bytes straight from a public bucket with range requests, neither has a server. They look like the same kind of thing and they are built on opposite assumptions about what a picture of data is made of.

gridlook’s assumption: the grid is the primitive. A dataset is a list of cells with values, and the job is to put each cell where it belongs. There is no image, only geometry carrying colour.

ortho-cog-viewer’s assumption: the image is the primitive. A dataset is a raster with a coordinate system and a geotransform, and the job is to move that raster into the view. Values never move; the mesh under them does.

Call them cell and warp. The sidebyside pages put one dataset in front of both, name the gap, and propose the bridge. This post is about why the gaps fall where they do, and why the two were never really separate.

Geometry is a recipe either way

The first thing to notice is that neither side stores coordinates.

A HEALPix cell has no stored position. Its id, together with the refinement level and the indexing scheme, is enough to compute its centre, its corners, its neighbours, its parent, all by arithmetic. When rangefinder first tried to open the EERIE store it went looking for a coordinate array named after the cell dimension and got three 404s, because there is none: the dimension is nameless on purpose.

A raster with a geotransform has no stored positions either. Six numbers and a CRS generate the position of every pixel on demand. Nobody writes down where pixel (4000, 2000) is; the recipe says.

So warp and cell are siblings. Both derive geometry late from a small description, and they differ only in what the description indexes: a regular lattice in a projected plane, or a hierarchical partition of the sphere. The odd one out is the third stance, the explicit one, where coordinates are stored and shipped: Simple Features, GeoArrow, a GeoParquet of polygons. That is the materialised answer to a question someone already asked, and it has its place, but it is not where the viewers live.

This is the recipe-not-payload principle showing up as a rendering taxonomy. The question to ask of any viewer is: how small a description generates how much geometry, and how late?

Drape is not warp

The second thing to notice is that “warp” names two different operations, and conflating them hides the most useful distinction in the whole comparison.

A materialised warp resamples the source into a target grid. The output is a new array with its own CRS and geotransform. You can read values from it, write it to a file, cache it, hand it to the next step. GDAL’s warper does this; rwarp does this; a MUR SST day published with 2x, 4x and 8x coarser siblings is this. New numbers come out.

A visual warp leaves the values alone and moves the geometry under them. The source stays a texture; the mesh carries target-CRS positions and the UVs point back into untouched pixels; the GPU samples at draw time and nothing is ever written down. ortho-cog-viewer does this. You can pick a value on screen, but you get it by inverting the mapping and reading the source, not by reading the picture.

The second is a drape, and a drape is exactly what gridlook does with cells: values as read, geometry derived late, picture as a side effect. So within the sidebyside suite, ortho-cog-viewer and gridlook are closer to each other than ortho-cog-viewer is to rwarp. rwarp is the only thing in the suite that produces data rather than a view.

That matters for the bridges. “Publish coarser siblings so gridlook can show a 650-million-cell field” is a materialised warp, done once by the data owner. “Sample HEALPix cells into a projected view” is a drape, done every frame by the viewer. The GPU interpolation in a drape is still a resampling; it is just one nobody can audit or reuse. A materialised warp costs a decision up front (kernel, nodata, alignment) and what comes out is a thing. A drape is cheap and honest and you cannot hand it to anyone.

Where the gaps fall

With those two distinctions in hand, the suite’s gaps stop looking like a feature list and start looking like consequences.

Cell-side gaps: no COG as data, no spatial windowing, no tile services, no projected CRS beyond what d3-geo offers. Every one of these follows from “the grid is the primitive”. A COG in UTM is an image, not a cell list. A tile service is images. Windowing is an image operation. If your primitive is cells on a sphere, level of detail has to come from the data owner, as a hierarchy of stores, because there is nothing to window.

Warp-side gaps, as of the work done in September and October 2026: no HEALPix, no ICON, no cells of any kind. Every one follows from “the image is the primitive”. A list of cells is not an image, and until something turns it into one (a mesh, or an inverse mapping from view pixels to cell ids) the warp renderers cannot see it.

Then there are the gaps that do not follow from either stance. Icechunk in rangefinder was one: not a consequence of anything, just a reader not yet written, and it landed in a day once named. Those are the cheap bridges, and the suite exists partly to make them stand out from the expensive ones.

HEALPix turned out to be nearly as cheap, for a reason the stance predicts. A HEALPix grid has an inverse: for any longitude and latitude the cell id is a closed computation. So the warp side can treat it the way it treats an affine grid, sending each view pixel to a cell id and reading the chunk that cell falls in. No mesh needed. gridlook builds a mesh and draws cells; rangefinder inverts the view and samples. Same geometry library underneath (healpix-geo), two routes to the picture. That page went from a gap to shared ground in a day too.

The one dataset both sides drew from the start is a CMIP6 tripolar ocean grid. gridlook places each cell on the sphere from its 2D longitude and latitude arrays. rangefinder takes the same arrays, computes cell corners, rasterises the cells into an affine view grid, and warps that. Same field, same month, two routes. The stances are not two worlds, they are two ends of one road, and a curvilinear grid happens to be reachable from both.

Modal thinking, and a 2017 post

Why does it feel like two worlds? Because tools carry models, and a community organises its thinking around the model its tools hold.

In 2017 I wrote a summary of R spatial that said, in effect: sf is here, it replaces sp and rgdal and rgeos, and this is good. It was. But the thing sp had done to us is worth naming now. sp made the vector/raster split a type system: SpatialPoints, SpatialLines, SpatialPolygons on one side, SpatialGrid and SpatialPixels on the other. SpatialPixels was the attempt to have it both ways, a raster that was secretly a table of cells with coordinates, and it fused two independent properties, whether the cells lie on a regular lattice and whether all of them are present, so it could represent neither cleanly. The lesson the community drew was “rasters and vectors are different things”, when the lesson available was that one type had conflated two ideas. sf then sharpened the vector side and left the raster side to raster and later terra, and the split became two package ecosystems with different maintainers, different idioms and a conversion function between them.

That is modal thinking: not wrong, just a habit of mind inherited from a data structure. The same thing is visible today in the two viewer worlds. The Earth system model community’s tools say the grid is the data, and so its people see images as a lossy export. The imagery community’s tools say the image is the data, and so its people see cells as an exotic grid type. Neither is a position anyone argued for. Each is what the tools made obvious.

The 2017 post ended with what sf could not represent: tracks, meshes, networks. Nine years on, the list has a new entry, and it is the same entry in a new coat: a discrete global grid is an indexed mesh whose indices are so good you never need to store the mesh.

What this is not

It is not an argument that one stance should win. The cell side is faster to a picture and more honest about what a cell is; the warp side degrades gracefully across data shapes the cell side cannot touch, and it can produce outputs rather than views. Both will keep being built, because the model centres will build cell viewers and the imagery centres will build warp viewers.

What it is: an argument for keeping the seam visible. Both sides now use the same libraries underneath (zarrita for chunks, icechunk-js for repositories, healpix-geo for cell geometry), so the difference is not in the reading, it is in what happens after. A viewer that lets you see which stance it is taking, and switch, is more useful than one that hides it. The sidebyside pages are a small way of insisting on that, and in their first week they worked less as a comparison than as a plan: name a gap in terms a page can show, write the bridge beside it, and the gap closes because the work was already specified.

Sources

  • The pages: mdsumner.github.io/sidebyside, with the bridge plans under docs/
  • gridlook (DKRZ and MPI-M; Fast, Koelling, Wachsmann, Kluft)
  • rangefinder, ortho-cog-viewer and rwarp (hypertidy / mdsumner)
  • Datasets and models: EERIE, ICON, MUR SST
  • Shared libraries underneath both viewers: zarrita, icechunk-js, healpix-geo, Icechunk, d3-geo
  • R spatial in 2017: this site, 2017-01-10

item.title: Small contracts, long lives: altarr and the shape of lazy arrays in R
item.dc:creator: Michael Sumner
item.description:
A few days ago I wrote about what R does today with an ALTREP that has a dim and no class. That post was about one mechanism: a lazy array, with no class and no methods, that base R indexing reads in planned batches. This post is about what happened next, which is that the mechanism turned out to be the missing piece in a handful of packages I had been building for years without quite knowing what they were waiting for.

The short version:

  • R has had the right array semantics for decades. What it lacked was a way to put a remote, chunked store behind them without a class.
  • altarr supplies that with one function, fetch(chunks). Everything else (Zarr, NetCDF, GDAL, HTTP, Rust) is somebody else’s engine.
  • In a few days that contract went into zaro, tidync and ndr with no changes to altarr itself.
  • Python’s cloud array stack is converging on the same shape: narrow interfaces over Rust and async engines. R can meet it there, cheaply, without rebuilding the engines.
  • The one change that would make this work for every lazy array in R is a small hook in R itself. That is a sustainability question as much as a technical one, and it is being asked at a good time.

The contract

Here is the whole interface between an altarr and whatever holds the data:

fetch(chunks)
# chunks:  integer matrix, one row per chunk, 0-based chunk coordinates
# returns: list of vectors, column-major, clipped at the array edge

x <- altarr(dim, chunk, fetch, type = "double")

The array is a plain double (or integer, or logical) vector with a dim. dim(x) reads nothing, x[cbind(i, j, k)] arrives at the fetch as one batch of chunks, saveRDS(x) writes the recipe rather than the values, and altarr_plan(x, i, j, k) returns the chunks a subscript would touch as a table. The previous post measured the difference: 192 round trips down to 1 for a region, 287 down to 1 for scattered points.

What matters for this post is not the speed but the size of the seam. One function, one matrix in, one list out. That is small enough that very different packages can each implement it in an afternoon, and small enough that it is unlikely to need changing.

A week of plugging things in

zaro is my Zarr reader built on Arrow’s filesystems and codecs, with Kerchunk and VirtualiZarr Parquet references. Its fetch_chunk() and decode_chunk() already were the altarr contract in all but name, so zaro_array(store, path), now exported from zaro, is about thirty lines. Zarr’s C-order shape is given to R reversed, so each decoded chunk lands in place with no aperm(). That is also faster than zaro’s own eager zaro_read(), which transposes every chunk.

tidync has always separated the plan (hyper_filter()) from the read (hyper_array()). An experimental branch adds hyper_array(lazy = TRUE), which returns altarrs using the NetCDF chunk sizes, and lets a chunk span several source files. tidync users get lazy arrays without learning a new object.

ndr is my named-dimension array package, an xarray-shaped layer with coordinates on axes. It had grown its own LazyDataArray class and a collect() step. With an altarr in Variable@data, that class goes away: ds$var costs nothing, isel() and sel() compose into a new lazy view, and reductions stream over chunk-aligned blocks. altarr’s own stated limit is coordinates (dimnames must be character); ndr is a coordinate layer. They fill each other’s gaps.

GDAL7 is the generated GDAL bindings package, and it is the broadest backend of all. read_mdarray() already returned dims reversed with nothing moved, so all it needed was the MDArray block size and advise_read(). Now as_altarr() takes an MDArray, a band (or an overview of one, via get_overview()), or a path and array name, and each fetch does one bounding read for the whole batch. So every GDAL multidimensional source (NetCDF, HDF5, GRIB, Zarr, Kerchunk Parquet, VRT, and soon Icechunk) is a plain R array. adgl, the plan-verbs layer over GDAL7, keeps its own overview-aware proxy for plotting, and gets its missing multidimensional story from ndr objects backed by GDAL7 altarrs.

None of these needed a change to altarr. The ndr work produced two nice-to-haves (an exported chunk-shape accessor, and a way to compose a view from an existing array’s recipe), and that is all.

The demo that made it real

I have a virtual Zarr of BRAN2023, the Bluelink ocean reanalysis: daily ocean temperature as one int16 array of 5479 x 51 x 1500 x 3600 (time, depth, lat, lon), 2010 to 2024. It is not stored as Zarr at all. It is a Kerchunk Parquet reference store on GitHub pointing at the monthly NetCDF files on NCI’s THREDDS server.

Extracting values along an animal track or a voyage is the classic job here: one value per (lon, lat, depth, time) position. With zaro opening the references and altarr presenting the array, the whole extraction is one line of base R:

temp <- zaro_array(store, "temp")      # lazy, nothing read
dim(temp)                              # 3600 1500 51 5479
track$temp <- temp[cbind(i, j, k, l)]  # one planned batch

That one subscript becomes one call to fetch, which resolves the chunk references and issues the byte-range requests through a single curl pool capped at 8 connections, which is what the THREDDS server can bear. Here is a made-up 30-day track off eastern Tasmania, one point per day in March 2023, diving from 5 m to 200 m, run against the real server:

                time   lon    lat depth  temp    i   j  k    l
 2023-03-01 12:00:00 147.8 -43.50     5 16.86 1478 315  1 4808
 2023-03-02 12:00:00 148.0 -43.34     6 17.09 1480 317  2 4809
 2023-03-03 12:00:00 148.1 -43.19     7 17.78 1482 319  2 4810
 ...
 2023-03-28 12:00:00 152.2 -39.31   198 12.86 1522 357 24 4835
 2023-03-29 12:00:00 152.3 -39.16   199 14.42 1524 359 24 4836
 2023-03-30 12:00:00 152.5 -39.00   200 13.76 1525 360 24 4837

mode=real max_con=8
metadata + coords + shard: 0.44 s
chunks planned: 30, altarr fetch calls: 1
byte-range requests to data server: 30 in 1 batch(es), 1954.6 KB, 0.52 s
track extract wall time: 1.95 s

Thirty chunks, one fetch call, thirty range requests to THREDDS in one capped batch: about 2 MB and half a second for the data, under 2 seconds end to end from a cold start, out of an array of more than 1.5 trillion values. The metadata, coordinates and the one manifest shard this track needs come from GitHub; only the chunk bytes come from NCI.

The thing to notice is where the politeness lives. The connection cap, the reference resolution and the HTTP are all inside the fetch. Base R’s indexing never knows. I used ff to do this exact job, ocean model against elephant seal tracks, in my thesis fifteen-odd years ago, with local files and a lot of code. It is the same question, now asked of a remote archive with one subscript.

Lazy before altarr: gdalraster and terra

None of this started with altarr. R has long had lazy access in practice, through database connections and the NetCDF APIs, but it was dbplyr and the tidyverse, and ALTREP after that, that gave laziness a name in R and got it widely developed. On the raster side, the foundation everything above stands on is GDAL access that holds a handle and reads only what is asked for.

gdalraster (Chris Toney and contributors) is, today, the best-practice way to use GDAL from R, and the one I recommend. A GDALRaster object is an open dataset handle and nothing more: opening reads metadata, and read() takes a window and an output size, so GDAL picks the overview and reads only the blocks it needs. Its stated design leans “toward minimalism and the use of simple, lightweight objects for holding raw data”. That is the same instinct as altarr: hold the handle, keep the plan cheap, and let the data be a plain vector when it arrives. gdalraster also already exposes GDAL’s multidimensional API (mdim_info(), mdim_translate()), the VSI virtual filesystems and vector layers.

terra (Robert Hijmans) works the same way for users: a SpatRaster points to file sources, and most operations run block by block in C++, writing to disk when a result will not fit in memory. Its laziness lives inside a C++ class with its own algebra, so the values surface as an R vector only when asked for.

altarr does not replace either. It adds the piece neither aims to be: an array that is an R vector, so that base indexing and any function written for arrays read it lazily. The natural constructor is the same one GDAL7’s as_altarr() uses for a band (chunk equals the band block size, fetch reads the bounding window and slices per block), and gdalraster is where that constructor would reach real users now. GDAL7 is the experimental, generated binding where I try out the whole API surface, including the multidimensional block size and AdviseRead calls the fetch wants; I have not settled how the two should share that work, and I would rather it be a conversation than a fork.

The same shape, four more times

Looking back over the last year, altarr is the R-side instance of a pattern I keep landing on: separate the plan from the read, make the plan a small, inspectable table, and let the engine be swappable.

  • rwarp is a Rust implementation of GDAL’s warp pipeline, split into plan, read and warp stages. collect_chunk_list answers “which source blocks does each target chunk need” before any pixel is touched, and the read is the caller’s job: a COG, a Zarr store, a Parquet byte-reference store. It builds for wasm32 with a pure-Rust PROJ backend.
  • ortho-cog-viewer (live) is a CRS-agnostic COG viewer: orthographic globes, polar stereographic, Goode homolosine, all reading COGs and tile servers straight from the browser. Its architecture puts a RasterSource with “fetch planning” on one side and a LayerEngine on the other, and the second engine is rwarp compiled to wasm: mesh reprojection while the view moves, a real warp once it settles.
  • rangefinder is a static, server-free Sentinel-2 explorer that reads COGs by HTTP range request and composes imagery in the browser. Its design is four layers (space, time, pixels, render), where the first three are interfaces and only the fourth is the product. Its notes already list Zarr as “a different layer 3”.
  • aatgrid is the space layer made explicit: a hierarchical tile grid for the Australian Antarctic Territory, aligned to Sentinel-2, with tile ids that resolve to UTM extents by arithmetic. It is an R package and a static explorer that share the same grid logic, and rangefinder’s design names it as a consumer of the same pixel library.

The R-to-browser path is not only imagery. The allboa projects (aobview, aobcore, scenespec) are an early modern mapview where R sends a renderer-neutral scene spec and Arrow buffers, and the browser fetches remote COGs itself. R describes; the engine reads.

An altarr fetch, an rwarp chunk list, an ortho-cog-viewer fetch plan and a rangefinder pixel source are the same idea at different layers: chunk coordinates in, values out, and a plan you can look at first. That is what makes the R packages and the browser tools one family rather than a pile of projects. A plan computed in R can be handed to the browser, or to Rust, and the bytes fetched wherever is cheapest.

Meanwhile, in Python

The Python geospatial array world has moved fast in the last two years, and the direction is worth naming, because it is the same direction.

  • Rust engines under thin Python. Development Seed built obstore over Rust’s object_store crate, reporting 9x the throughput of fsspec for concurrent small requests, and zarr-python now uses it. async-geotiff, on the Rust async-tiff core, exists because “by leveraging asynchronous I/O, we can speed up concurrent GeoTIFF data fetching”, a gap they name in GDAL and rasterio.
  • Zarr as the meeting point. zarr-python 3, Development Seed’s “Zarr everywhere” work, and zarrs, a full Zarr v3 implementation in Rust from the ANU here in Australia, which also ships a codec pipeline for zarr-python.
  • Virtual and versioned stores. VirtualiZarr 2.0 (July 2025) added pluggable parsers and a ManifestStore, so archival NetCDF and HDF5 become Zarr without copying. Icechunk reached 1.0 in July 2025 and 2.0 in April 2026, with variable-length (rectilinear) chunk grids following in May.
  • Companies carrying the core. Earthmover, founded by xarray and Zarr leads, raised a $7.2M seed round in September 2025 for Icechunk, Arraylake and Flux. Development Seed is a consultancy whose open-source work is funded project by project.

The lesson I take is not “rewrite it in Rust”. It is that the winning pieces are narrow: obstore has about a dozen methods; a Kerchunk or Icechunk manifest is a table of chunk keys and byte ranges; a VirtualiZarr parser is one protocol. xarray sits on top, and the engines underneath are interchangeable.

R does not need to rebuild those engines. GDAL already reads Zarr v3, Kerchunk Parquet and, from 3.14, Icechunk. Rust crates are reachable through extendr. What R needed was the narrow piece on its side of the boundary: a way to make an engine’s chunks look like an ordinary R array. That is altarr’s job, and it is why it is small.

Other threads in R

altarr is not the only lazy array story in R, and it should not try to be.

  • DelayedArray and HDF5Array in Bioconductor are the most complete answer to lazy compute on arrays in R, and Bioconductor now has ZarrArray (Hervé Pagès, April 2026), which brings Zarr in through Rarr as a DelayedArray. An altarr can be a DelayedArray seed, since extract_array() is altarr_extract(), and that gives altarr delayed operations for free.
  • The zarr package from R-CF is a native, extensible Zarr v3 driver on CRAN. An altarr view over its arrays is a natural offer.
  • arrow and vroom proved ALTREP at scale for columns; stars proxies and gdalcubes have their own laziness inside their own classes, as terra does (above).

The difference is still the class. Every package above is an object with methods, so code must know about it. An altarr has no class, so code written in 1998 reads it lazily. The approaches stack: lazy reads underneath, any of these for lazy compute above.

Sustaining R, one small hook at a time

On 6 October the R Consortium hosts Sustaining R: Investing in the People, Infrastructure, and Community Behind R, with Simon Urbanek, Kurt Hornik and Heather Turner. The context is real money and real limits: the Sovereign Tech Fund put $450,000 into the R Foundation in October 2025 to modernize R’s core infrastructure, and the Research Software Maintenance Fund GBP 500,000 grant (December 2025) aims to grow the next generation of contributors to R itself, with R Core mentoring. Both are time-limited, and the R blog says plainly that “there is a continued need to raise funds for long-term sustainability”.

Python’s array stack is carried by funded companies and large grant programs. R’s is carried by a small core team, CRAN, and a long tail of people like me maintaining packages around a day job. That is not a complaint; it is the constraint, and it suggests a strategy.

The strategy is small contracts. A language with a small core team lasts by keeping its interfaces few, stable and general, so that packages and engines can come and go around them without breaking users. R’s indexing is exactly such an interface: x[i, j, k] and x[cbind(i, j, k)] mean what they meant in S. ALTREP is another. altarr adds one more at the package level, fetch(chunks), and asks R for one more at the base level:

/* in ArraySubset / MatrixSubset, after subscripts are normalized */
if (ALTREP(x)) {
    SEXP ans = ALTVEC_EXTRACT_ARRAY_SUBSET(x, subs, call);
    if (ans != NULL) { /* attach dim and dimnames as today */ }
}

That hook adds no data model and no new class. It would turn x[i, j, k] into one planned request for every ALTREP array in R, from arrow to gdalraster to whatever comes next, and it falls back to today’s behaviour for every class that does not implement it. It is the kind of contribution to R itself that these programs are trying to make possible: small, measured (altarr is the test bed, and the tests check every path against base R with identical()), and useful far beyond the package that motivated it.

I think that is a better model for sustaining R than trying to match Python feature for feature. Keep the base small and sound. Push engines out to GDAL, Rust and the browser, where others already maintain them. Spend scarce R effort on the thin layer where R’s own semantics meet those engines, because that layer is what only R people can build, and it is what makes forty years of R code work on data that did not exist when it was written.

What next

  1. Build R-devel with the ArraySubset hook and show x[i, j, k] going from 192 round trips to 1 with no package method, then take it to R-devel and the people who know subset.c best.
  2. Land the backends: zaro and tidync on CRAN-ready branches once altarr is on CRAN, ndr on altarr, a block-based altarr over a gdalraster GDALRaster (offered to gdalraster rather than forked), alongside GDAL7’s as_altarr() for the multidimensional side.
  3. A concurrent fetch off the R thread (GDAL AdviseRead, or Rust object_store) so every backend gets it at once.
  4. The BRAN2023 track extraction as a worked example in zaro, with longer tracks and more variables.
  5. A Zarr pixel layer for rangefinder and ortho-cog-viewer, sharing the chunk plan with rwarp.

If you maintain a lazy array package in R, or know subset.c well, I would very much like to hear from you.

Links

  • altarr: https://github.com/hypertidy/altarr
  • zaro: https://github.com/hypertidy/zaro, ndr: https://github.com/mdsumner/ndr, tidync: https://github.com/ropensci/tidync
  • GDAL7: https://github.com/rgdal-dev/GDAL7, adgl: https://github.com/rgdal-dev/adgl
  • rwarp: https://github.com/hypertidy/rwarp, rangefinder: https://hypertidy.github.io/rangefinder/
  • ortho-cog-viewer: https://github.com/mdsumner/ortho-cog-viewer, aatgrid: https://github.com/mdsumner/aatgrid, allboa: https://github.com/allboa
  • gdalraster: https://firelab.github.io/gdalraster/, terra: https://rspatial.github.io/terra/
  • BRAN2023 virtual store: https://github.com/mdsumner/virtualized/tree/main/remote
  • R Consortium, Sustaining R webinar (6 Oct 2026): https://github.com/RConsortium/rconsortium_website/blob/main/webinars/sustaining-r-investing-in-the-people-infrastructure-and-community.qmd
  • Sovereign Tech Fund investment in the R Foundation: https://r-consortium.org/posts/sovereign-tech-fund-invests-450000-in-r-foundation-to-enhance-r-sustainability-and-security/
  • RSMF, enabling the next generation of contributors to R: https://blog.r-project.org/2025/12/17/rsmf-enabling-the-next-generation-of-contributors-to-r/
  • obstore: https://developmentseed.org/blog/2025-08-01-obstore/; async-geotiff: https://developmentseed.org/async-geotiff/latest/blog/2026/02/03/introducing-async-geotiff/
  • Zarr everywhere (Development Seed): https://developmentseed.org/blog/2025-10-13-zarr/
  • VirtualiZarr releases: https://virtualizarr.readthedocs.io/en/stable/about/releases.html; Icechunk blog: https://icechunk.io/en/latest/blog-posts/
  • zarrs: https://docs.rs/crate/zarrs/latest
  • Earthmover seed round: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250919639500/en/
  • ZarrArray (Bioconductor): https://bioconductor.org/packages/ZarrArray/

item.title: What R does today with an ALTREP that has a dim and no class
item.dc:creator: Michael Sumner
item.description:
Base R can already read a remote, chunked, compressed array in planned batches, using nothing but its own indexing syntax. The object has no class and no methods: it is a double vector with a dim attribute. One of R’s indexing forms reaches it as a single planned request today; another reaches it one element at a time; and a small change to R would close that gap.

I wanted to know how far R’s old and very rich array indexing could go as a query language for remote encoded chunks, without patching R. So I built altarr, a small ALTREP prototype, read through src/main/subset.c to see what each indexing form actually does, and measured it. Then I pointed it at a real Zarr store written by zarr-python.

The short version: x[cbind(i, j, k)] is already first-class. x[i, j, k] works, but serially. And the information R would need to fix that is already sitting in a local variable inside ArraySubset.

Two kinds of array question

There are two different things you can ask of a 3-d array with three index vectors. The orthogonal question asks for every combination: a hyperslab, the outer product of the indices. The pointwise question pairs the indices up: the first i with the first j with the first k, giving one value per point. A chunked store cares a lot about which one you mean, because they touch completely different sets of chunks.

R and numpy chose opposite defaults:

R numpy zarr-python
orthogonal (hyperslab) x[i, j, k] x[np.ix_(i, j, k)] z.oindex[i, j, k]
pointwise (points) x[cbind(i, j, k)] x[i, j, k] with integer arrays z.vindex[i, j, k]

Zarr grew two named accessors, oindex and vindex, to say what S and R have said in base syntax for decades. xarray meets the same split as orthogonal versus vectorized isel. I checked the table against a real store: on the Zarr array used later in this post, z.vindex[[29, 14], [49, 24], [69, 34]] and R’s x[cbind(c(70, 35), c(50, 25), c(30, 15))] both return 104999 50714, and z.oindex returns the same 8 values as R’s x[i, j, k]. (The R indices are reversed and 1-based; more on why below.)

Matrix indexing is one of the least appreciated parts of R. It long predates lazy evaluation in most of the places people now care about it, and as it turns out, it is exactly the form that reaches a lazy array as a single, plannable request.

What R does with it

ALTREP (since R 3.5) lets a package supply a vector whose contents come from somewhere other than a block of memory. The package registers methods: Length, Elt for one element, Extract_subset for a set of indices, Dataptr for a pointer to all the data. R’s own code calls them instead of reading memory. To R, the result is just a vector.

So what happens when that vector has a dim attribute and you index it? Reading src/main/subset.c (R 4.3 and current trunk have the same structure), there are three paths:

you write R calls the ALTREP object sees can it plan?
x[i] VectorSubset then ExtractSubset Extract_subset(x, indx), every index at once yes
x[cbind(i, j, k)] mat2indsub then ExtractSubset Extract_subset(x, indx), every index at once yes
x[i, j, k] ArraySubset or MatrixSubset Elt(x, offset), one element at a time no
x + 1, print(x) anything needing the data pointer Dataptr(x) must materialize

Matrix indexing is converted to linear indices before it reaches ALTREP, but the whole set arrives in one call. That is enough: the object can recover each index’s chunk, find the unique chunks, and fetch them together.

The rectangular form is the surprise. ArraySubset normalizes each subscript with int_arraySubscript() and holds the result in a local array, subs[k]: one integer vector per dimension. That is the hyperslab, exactly. But it never offers subs to ALTREP. It loops over the result in column-major order and calls REAL_ELT() once per element.

altarr: the experiment

altarr is a small R package with a C core. altarr(dim, chunk, fetch) returns a lazy array: a double vector, a dim attribute, no class. Values arrive chunk by chunk from a fetch function you supply, so the store behind it can be object storage, Zarr, GDAL, or a generator in a test.

The whole contract with the store is one function:

fetch(chunks)
# chunks:  integer matrix, one row per chunk, one column per dimension,
#          0-based chunk coordinates
# returns: list of numeric vectors, one per row, column-major,
#          clipped at the array edge

A call to fetch is one round trip, however many chunks it asks for. The ALTREP methods do the rest:

  • Elt finds the element’s chunk, fetches it alone if it is not cached, and returns one value.
  • Extract_subset maps every index to its chunk, fetches all the uncached chunks in one call, then assembles.
  • Dataptr materializes the whole array, and refuses above getOption("altarr.max_materialize", 1e6) values.

Here is a lazy 1440 x 720 x 365 array (378 million values, never allocated) from a generator with 20 ms of latency per call:

library(altarr)
d  <- c(1440L, 720L, 365L)
cs <- c(60L, 60L, 10L)
remote <- function(chunks) {
  Sys.sleep(0.02)                     # one round trip
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(chunks)), function(r) {
    st <- chunks[r, ] * cs + 1L
    en <- pmin(st + cs - 1L, d)
    as.vector(outer(outer(st[1]:en[1], 1e4 * (st[2]:en[2]), "+"),
                    1e8 * (st[3]:en[3]), "+"))
  })
}
x <- altarr(d, cs, remote)
class(x)           # "array"
is.object(x)       # FALSE
altarr_stats(x)    # counts Elt calls, fetch calls, chunks

altarr_stats() counts what R actually asked for, which is how the numbers below were measured.

Measured

On the 378-million-value array, the planned paths read the same chunks as the element-at-a-time paths in a single round trip, and are 20 to 40 times faster.

The latency stands in for an object-store GET, with a batch of chunks assumed to be fetched concurrently. A linear slice, x[1:1e5], also goes through Extract_subset: 48 chunks in 1 call. Point extraction through x[cbind(...)] is already first-class in unpatched R; the rectangular form is correct and lazy, but serial.

A real Zarr store

A generator proves the mechanics; a real store proves the contract is enough. zarr-python wrote a Zarr v2 array of shape (30, 50, 70), chunks (7, 16, 20), zlib-compressed, C order. The chunk shape is ragged at every edge, and one chunk is entirely fill value, so the store simply omits its file.

altarr_zarr_v2() reads .zarray and implements fetch in about 85 lines of plain R: build the chunk key, read the file (or return fill_value if it is missing), memDecompress(), readBin(), and clip Zarr’s padded edge chunks.

z <- altarr_zarr_v2("zdemo.zarr")
dim(z)                                        # 70 50 30
z[cbind(c(70, 35), c(50, 25), c(30, 15))]     # 104999 50714, one fetch call
altarr_extract(z, , , )                       # every value, one fetch call

Every value matches zarr-python’s array exactly, including the omitted chunk and the clipped edges.

The dimensions come out reversed, and that is deliberate. A C-order array of shape (s1, …, sn) has bytes that are already column-major for shape (sn, …, s1). So altarr gives R dim c(70, 50, 30) and decodes each chunk straight into place, with no transposition at all. R’s x[i, j, k] on that array is zarr’s z.oindex[k, j, i], shifted by one.

A real dataset, with GDAL doing the hard parts

The zarr-python store keeps the package self-contained. For real data, the classic xarray tutorial air_temperature dataset is published as Zarr over HTTP, compressed with Blosc. A Blosc decoder and an HTTP range-reader are exactly the things altarr should not grow, so GDAL does both in one command:

gdal mdim convert \
  "ZARR:\"/vsicurl/https://scottyhq.github.io/zarrdata/air_temperature.zarr/\"" \
  air_temperature.zarr --co FORMAT=ZARR_V2 --co ARRAY:COMPRESS=ZLIB

The result is a local, zlib-compressed Zarr v2 store, and the same reader opens it:

x <- altarr_zarr_v2("air_temperature.zarr/air")
dim(x)                 # 53 x 25 x 2920: lon, lat, time
                       # int16, chunks 27 x 13 x 730, 16 of them

x[20, 10, ]            # a time series at one cell, in kelvin
                       # orthogonal: Elt path, 4 chunks in 4 round trips
altarr_extract(x, 20, 10, )      # the same 4 chunks in 1 round trip

x[cbind(lon_i, lat_i, time_i)]   # a track, one time per position
                                 # pointwise: one planned batch

Those are the two questions from the start of this post, on real data. The time series sits under one cell, so it touches the 4 time chunks there: 4 round trips today, 1 with the hook. A 500-point track spread over the year touches all 16 chunks, and already arrives as a single request.

air is stored as int16 with a scale factor of 0.01. altarr_zarr_v2() applies the CF packing attributes from .zattrs (scale_factor, add_offset, _FillValue) inside fetch, so values arrive in kelvin and fill values become NA. Unpacking is a concern of the fetch, not of the ALTREP layer.

This is also the point to resist building a Zarr engine. Remote I/O, Blosc, sharding, Zarr v3 codecs and their combinations are a never-ending road, and every step along it is a detour from the question here. The fetch contract exists so the engine can be someone else’s: GDAL as a converter in this example, and the natural next step is a fetch that calls GDAL’s multidimensional API, or object_store and the Rust codec crates, directly. The ALTREP layer only needs chunk coordinates in and values out.

What comes for free

Because the object is an ordinary vector to R, a lot of behaviour arrives without any code:

  • Shape is free. dim(), length() and str() read nothing.
  • Copy-on-modify works. y <- x; y[1, 1, 1] <- 0 materializes y only; x stays lazy and unchanged.
  • R’s own wrapper keeps the planning. Changing an attribute on a shared object (dimnames(y) <- ... after y <- x) makes R wrap it in its internal wrapper ALTREP class. The wrapper forwards Extract_subset, so matrix indexing still arrives as one planned request.
  • Serialization stores the recipe, not the payload. ALTREP has a Serialized_state method, so saveRDS() of the 378-million-value array writes 1250 bytes: dim, chunk shape and fetch function. For the Zarr array it is 3.7 KB, and readRDS() in a fresh R session loads the package and returns a lazy array that reads from the store on first use.
  • The plan is a table. altarr_plan(x, i, j, k) returns the chunks a subscript would touch, one row per chunk, with 0-based chunk coordinates, starts and extents. The plan is a table, and the array is what assembling it gives you.

That last point connects to an older thread. A chunk manifest (Icechunk’s, kerchunk’s, a COG’s tile index) is already a table of chunk keys to byte ranges. Chunk extents are min/max statistics for free, so filtering that table on coordinates is chunk pruning without anyone computing statistics.

The hook R could add

ExtractSubset already does this for vectors: if the object is ALTREP, it offers the indices to the class’s Extract_subset method first, and falls back to the element loop only if the method returns NULL. The same pattern would fit in ArraySubset and MatrixSubset, just after the subscripts are normalized and bounds-checked:

if (ALTREP(x)) {
    SEXP ans = ALTVEC_EXTRACT_ARRAY_SUBSET(x, s, call);  /* s: per-dim subs */
    if (ans != NULL) {
        /* attach dim and dimnames exactly as the existing code does */
    }
}
/* otherwise the element loop runs, as today */

The new method receives one normalized integer vector per dimension. Returning NULL keeps today’s behaviour, so nothing changes for any class that does not implement it.

altarr_extract(x, i, j, k) emulates this from package code: it normalizes each subscript with R’s own rules (by indexing a seq_len() of each dimension), plans the cartesian product of touched chunks, fetches once, and assembles. Its results are identical() to x[i, j, k] across negative, logical, character, NA, missing and zero-length subscripts, with and without drop.

The argument for the hook is that it is general. It adds no data model and no new object type, and every lazy array in R benefits: arrow, gdalraster, Zarr readers, anything ALTREP-backed with a shape.

Prior art, and what is different

Out-of-memory arrays in R are not new, and some of the older work was remarkably capable:

  • ff gave R memory-mapped, chunked vectors and arrays long before most languages had anything comparable, with its own [ methods doing the paging. (I used ff heavily in my own thesis, chapter 6 to map 4D ocean model to diving elephant seal movement estimates).
  • bigmemory offered shared and file-backed matrices for parallel work.
  • DelayedArray and HDF5Array in Bioconductor provide lazy, chunk-aware arrays with block processing and delayed operations, and are the most complete answer to lazy compute on arrays in R.
  • arrow and vroom use ALTREP to hand R vectors whose contents are not yet in R memory.

The difference here is the class. Every one of the array packages above is an S3 or S4 object with methods: code has to know about the class, or the object gets converted. An ALTREP array with a dim and no class needs no method dispatch at all. Any function that indexes a numeric array, written in 1998 or yesterday, reads it lazily, and matrix indexing reads it in one planned batch.

That is also the limit. Without a class there is nowhere to hang delayed arithmetic, which is where DelayedArray’s design earns its complexity. The two approaches fit together: lazy reads through base indexing underneath, lazy compute in a plan above.

Limits, and what next

This is a prototype, and the limits are real:

  • Lazy reads, not lazy compute. Anything that needs the data pointer (arithmetic, printing, most of apply) materializes the whole array. altarr refuses that above a size option rather than fetching 3 GB because someone typed x + 1.
  • The cache is unbounded. It holds one slot per chunk in the grid; it needs an LRU and a byte budget.
  • Fetch runs on R’s main thread. Concurrency belongs inside the fetch implementation (object_store in Rust, GDAL), never touching the R API off-thread. The fetch contract is where a Rust backend plugs in, without touching the ALTREP layer.
  • Coordinates are still dimnames, which must be character. ALTREP does not touch that; numeric coordinates are a separate question for base R.

Next steps:

  1. Build R-devel with the ArraySubset hook and show x[i, j, k] going from 192 round trips to 1, with no package-side method.
  2. A Rust fetch backend over object storage, so the demo reads a remote Zarr store rather than a local one.
  3. Ask the people who know ALTREP and R’s subscript code best whether the hook is sound.

The code, tests and the measurement script are in the altarr package . The tests check every path against base R with identical().

Links

  • R’s subsetting code: src/main/subset.c (GitHub mirror of the R sources)
  • numpy indexing, including np.ix_: https://numpy.org/doc/stable/user/basics.indexing.html
  • zarr-python: https://zarr.readthedocs.io/
  • The air_temperature Zarr store: https://scottyhq.github.io/zarrdata/air_temperature.zarr/
  • ff: https://cran.r-project.org/package=ff
  • DelayedArray: https://bioconductor.org/packages/DelayedArray/

item.title: A mapview for modern R: Arrow in, any CRS out
item.dc:creator: Michael Sumner
item.description:
R can have a fast, CRS-honest interactive map viewer, and GeoArrow is what makes it cheap to build now. The prompt is deckglgeoarrow, which landed on CRAN this year: it ships sf and wk data to the browser as GeoArrow and lets deck.gl draw it on the GPU, on a maplibre map built with mapgl.

That package is a good answer to “show me a lot of features fast on a web map”. This post asks a wider question. What would a mapview for modern R look like if it were not tied to one JavaScript library, and not tied to Web Mercator? And how should it be split between a lean core and the convenience layer that makes mapview so loved?

The short version:

  • Arrow does not give R and the browser shared memory, but it removes the parse. That is the real win.
  • Mercator is a basemap problem, not a GPU problem.
  • The core should be a protocol (data plane, scene spec, transport), not a widget.
  • Start on deck.gl, probe how far arbitrary CRS goes, and keep a clean seam so a capable team could own the renderer later.
  • Start on deck.gl, probe how far arbitrary CRS goes, and keep a clean seam so a capable team could own the renderer later.
NoteThis is now a real, early-stage project

The design below became allonboard: aobview is the mapview-style view(x) front door, aobcore is the core package and renderer, and scenespec is the renderer-neutral scene spec described below. Decisions live in design and experiments in spikes, all under the allboa GitHub organisation.

It is early and in the open: names are placeholders, nothing is on CRAN, and the scene spec is pre-1.0. view() already works for sf/terra vectors and rasters, draws in any projected CRS (lon/lat data south of 40°S goes to EPSG:3031, north of 60°N to EPSG:3413), fetches remote COGs in tiles, and supports colour-by-attribute, legends and popups. The open problems are the ones this post anticipated: seams and the antimeridian in some projections, tile budgets for large rasters, and whether the renderer ends up sharing lonboard’s JavaScript stack. Try it and open an issue — feedback is the most useful thing right now.

What Arrow actually changes

Arrow does not share memory between R and the page; it ships bytes the GPU can use without parsing them. R and the browser are separate processes, so data always crosses a boundary. What matters is how much work happens on the far side.

The classic mapview path was htmlwidgets. sf became GeoJSON text, the text was embedded in the page, and the browser parsed it into JS objects and then into Leaflet layers. Most of the cost was in that parse and in building millions of small objects. leafgl (WebGL drawing) and flatgeobuf attachments (binary, streamable) already moved away from it. GeoArrow is where that path was heading.

With GeoArrow, an Arrow IPC buffer becomes JS typed arrays with no parse. deck.gl-geoarrow binds those coordinate buffers straight into GPU attributes. The format is still serialized, but the cost is close to a memory copy, not a parse-and-build.

Two consequences follow:

  • True shared memory exists in webR. When R runs as wasm in the same page, Arrow buffers can be handed across without a copy. Designing around Arrow now keeps that door open.
  • The browser can fetch the data itself. deckglgeoarrow can already render remote GeoParquet and GeoArrow without reading it into R; only the styling is prepared in R (CRAN reference). R sends a recipe, the browser pulls the bytes.

One constraint shapes the core: only native GeoArrow geometry encoding renders, not WKB (README). The data plane must emit native coordinate buffers. A wk handler writing geoarrow does that, and so does GDAL’s OGR Arrow stream when asked for GeoArrow encoding, which keeps a gdalraster-to-browser path free of conversions.

Mercator is a basemap problem

The GPU does not care about Web Mercator; the tiled basemap does. deck.gl has orthographic and cartesian views, so projected metres can go straight in and render in any CRS. deckglgeoarrow is Mercator-bound only because it sits on mapgl and maplibre.
